chapterTitle: VM Memory Access: Push and Pop
aiGenerationNote:
Create an animated lesson showing the VM memory segments as a set of labeled drawers. Show the stack as a growing and shrinking pile of papers on a desk. Show push as taking a paper from a drawer and adding it to the pile. Show pop as taking a paper from the pile and filing it in a drawer. Show the constant segment as a virtual drawer that doesn't exist — the paper is created on the spot. Show the pointer segment as a drawer that controls which drawer is "this" and which is "that". Show the assembly code as a detailed filing instruction manual. End with a reflection: "Why does the VM have so many different memory segments instead of just one big memory?"

---

screens.title: VM Memory Access: Push and Pop
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how VM push and pop commands move data between the stack and named memory segments on the Hack platform. We'll make the mapping from virtual segments — local, argument, this, that, pointer, temp and static — to concrete R A M addresses clear, and you'll see why pushing a value is simpler than popping one. You'll study the assembly patterns used by a VM translator: how to compute base-plus-index addresses, how to write and read the stack, and how the translator uses a temporary register to solve pop's extra step. A practical outcome is that you will be able to implement push and pop for all segments and test them using the provided VM programs. Along the way we'll highlight common misconceptions, such as thinking the constant segment lives in R A M or that pop and push cost the same number of instructions. By the end, you should be confident mapping VM commands to assembly and explaining the asymmetry that makes pop more complex. Consider how a stack-based translator forces explicit address calculation — that idea will keep returning in later chapters.

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Push reads a source and stores it on the stack; pop computes a destination address first, then stores the popped value there. Each VM segment maps to a fixed or base-plus-offset RAM region.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › VM Memory Access
VM Memory Access: Push and Pop
Translate stack operations into Hack assembly by mapping VM segments to RAM and using a temporary register for pop.
In this lesson
Implement push/pop for all VM segments and verify with small VM programs.
Coming up
Learn assembly patterns, address computation, and static allocation by class.
Why this matters
A VM translator must produce correct memory accesses for functions and objects. Correct push/pop ensures variables, arguments, and object fields move reliably between memory and the stack during program execution.
Quick map
local → RAM[LCL + i]
temp → RAM[5 + i]
static → RAM[16 + i]
Visual concept
Drawers (segments)
Named segments map to drawers in RAM: local, argument, this, that.
Stack
A pile of values reachable via SP (RAM[0]). Push adds a paper; pop removes and files it.
Temporary slots
Fixed addresses for temp and pointer segments provide direct RAM access.
Concept map
Segments as Drawers
Each segment maps to a RAM region or fixed addresses.
Stack Pointer (SP)
SP refers to top of stack at RAM[0].
Pop vs Push
Push reads and writes to stack; pop must compute destination and use a temp register.
Explore Key Topics
Addressing
Compute base + index for local/argument/this/that.
Pointer & Temp
Pointer maps to RAM[3,4]; temp to RAM[5..12].
Static allocation
Static variables map from RAM[16] upward and are class-scoped.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This first objectives screen prepares you for the practical work ahead. First, you will implement the VM memory access commands push and pop so your translator moves values correctly between the stack and memory. That skill matters because functions, arguments, and object fields all depend on accurate memory access. A concrete example is translating a call to push local 2: it becomes assembly that computes LCL plus two, reads the value, and places it on the stack. Second, you will map every VM memory segment to its hardware location. Knowing that temp begins at R A M address five and that static variables begin at sixteen lets you generate fixed address code without guessing. These two objectives together let you produce correct assembly for a program's variable handling. A common misconception is to treat every segment identically; instead, segments differ in whether they are virtual, base-plus-index, fixed addresses, or per-class allocations. By mastering these two objectives you'll be positioned to implement and test push/pop across all segments.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: On this second objectives screen we'll deepen the practical expectations. You will learn to generate the exact assembly patterns for each push and pop variant, including the sequence of instructions to compute base addresses, read or write values, and update SP. For example, pushing from local requires loading LCL, adding the index, reading the value, and then writing it at R A M[SP] before incrementing SP; you'll produce that code reliably. You will also practice the pop sequence: compute and save the destination address in a temporary register, pop the topmost value from the stack into D, then store D at the saved address. This pattern avoids losing either the address or the value. Finally, you will test your translator with small VM programs that exercise constants, pointer adjustments, and local moves. A typical mistake is forgetting to use a temporary register for pop, which leads to wrong destination writes. Mastering these objectives ensures your translator produces correct and debuggable assembly.

screens.title: VM Memory Segments and Hardware Mapping
screens.narratorSegment: Begin by defining the named VM memory segments and their hardware mapping. The VM defines segments like local, argument, this and that as regions addressed by a base register plus an index. For example, local maps to R A M at address LCL plus index — written conceptually as R A M[LCL + index]. Argument similarly maps to R A M[ARG + index]. The pointer and temp segments instead map to fixed R A M addresses: pointer maps to R A M[3] and R A M[4] for index zero and one; temp begins at R A M[5] with offsets for each index. The static segment is special: it is a class-level collection mapped starting at R A M[16]. Static variables are given unique addresses and shared across instances of the same class. Finally, constant is a virtual segment — there is no R A M backing it. Pushing a constant creates the value in the instruction stream, not by reading memory. A useful mental model is labeled drawers: base-plus-offset drawers for local/argument/this/that, fixed-slot drawers for temp and pointer, and a global shelf starting at 16 for static. A common misconception is assuming constant must be read from memory; instead it is supplied directly. Think about why those differences exist: fixed slots are simple for temporary storage, base-plus-index supports variable-length frames, and static persists across calls. How will this mapping affect the translation code you write?

keyIdea.title: Segment Map
keyIdea.text: Local/argument/this/that are base-plus-index; pointer/temp are fixed addresses; static starts at RAM[16]; constant is virtual.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Segments & Mapping
Segment definitions
Each segment has a clear role and a concrete RAM mapping that your translator must use.
local
Mapped to RAM[LCL + index]. Stores function local variables.
argument
Mapped to RAM[ARG + index]. Holds parameters passed to the current function.
this / that
Base addresses for object fields or arrays: RAM[THIS + index], RAM[THAT + index].
pointer / temp
pointer → RAM[3 + i] (this/that); temp → RAM[5 + i] fixed slots.
static and constant
static → RAM[16 + index], class-scoped; constant is virtual — values embedded in instructions.
Hardware registers
Special registers are stored at fixed RAM locations and are central to address computation.
SP = RAM[0]
LCL = RAM[1]
ARG = RAM[2]
THIS = RAM[3], THAT = RAM[4]
Analogy
Think of base-plus-index segments as drawers in a filing cabinet that move when the base register changes. Temp and pointer are fixed cubbyholes, and static are labeled shelves starting at a fixed address.

screens.title: Push constant: assembly pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Pushing a constant illustrates how a virtual segment works. There is no memory read because the value is supplied by the VM command itself. The translation pattern loads the constant into the D register, writes D to the address pointed by SP, and then increments SP. Concretely, the translator emits assembly that places the numeric value into A, sets D to A, writes D into R A M[SP], and then increments SP. This is efficient because no base or index computation is needed. A common example is push constant 7: the translator simply creates the value seven and pushes it. A common misconception is trying to treat constant like static or local and reading R A M; that is unnecessary and incorrect. Practically, when you implement this, ensure the code uses A and D registers safely and always increments SP after storing the value. The visual code block shows the canonical assembly sequence so you can copy the pattern into your translator and test it. After testing, ask yourself why this pattern is shorter than most pop sequences and what that implies about runtime cost.

keyIdea.title: Push constant
keyIdea.text: Load the immediate value into D, write to RAM[SP], then increment SP — no memory read required.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Push constant
Assembly pattern
The translator emits a short, fixed instruction sequence for push constant.
@value
D=A
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1
This loads the literal value into D, stores it where SP points, and increments SP so the stack has the new top.
Explanation bullets
  • Load immediate value: @value then D=A places the constant in D.
  • Store at stack top: set A to RAM[SP] (A=M) and write M=D.
  • Advance SP: increment RAM[0] so the top moves up.
  • Why virtual: no RAM lookup is required for the constant segment.
Key Takeaway

Constants are embedded values; push constant requires only immediate load and stack write.

screens.title: Push from base-plus-index segments
screens.narratorSegment: Pushing from base-plus-index segments involves a predictable sequence: compute the address base plus index, read the value from that computed address into D, write D to the stack at SP, and increment SP. The base register might be LCL, ARG, THIS, or THAT depending on the segment. For example, push local 3 becomes code that loads LCL into D, adds the constant three to set A to LCL + 3, then reads M into D and pushes it. The essential steps are address computation, value read, stack store, and SP increment. When you implement this in your translator, avoid overwriting registers you still need; use the D register for intermediate values and use the A register to address memory. A common mistake is performing A=D+A while A is not set correctly — always ensure the base is in D or M as your chosen pattern requires. Another pitfall is forgetting to return A to the stack address before writing D. Test pushes by pushing known locals and then popping them to a fixed R A M slot to observe the values. This pattern is robust and repeated across multiple segments, which means once you implement one, it is straightforward to adapt for others.

keyIdea.title: Push base+index
keyIdea.text: Compute base register plus index to read a value, then push that value onto the stack and increment SP.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Push local/argument/this/that
Standard push sequence
Compute base plus index, read value, push to stack.
@LCL
D=M      // D = base address of local
@index
A=D+A    // A = LCL + index
D=M      // D = value at local[index]
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1
This template works for argument (use ARG), this (THIS), and that (THAT) by substituting the base register symbol.
Explanation bullet list
  • Load the base address register into D so we can add the index.
  • Add the index to compute the target address, then read M at that address.
  • Write the read value to RAM[SP] and increment SP to grow the stack.
  • Apply identical pattern for argument, this, and that with their respective base registers.
Common mistake

Mixing up D and A during address computation can point to the wrong RAM location; preserve the base correctly before adding the index.

screens.title: Pop into base-plus-index segments
screens.narratorSegment: Popping a value into a base-plus-index destination is more involved than pushing. The core problem is that computing the destination address and retrieving the popped value both require registers, but you cannot hold both in D simultaneously while addressing memory. The standard solution is to compute base + index, store that computed address in a temporary register such as R13, then pop the stack into D, and finally write D into the saved address. Concretely, you place the index into D, add LCL to get the target address, store that address in R13, decrement SP and move the popped value into D, then set A to R13 and store D there. This sequence guarantees you don't lose either piece of data. A common misconception is thinking you can compute the address after popping; doing so risks overwriting registers used to pop the value. When implementing, ensure you follow the sequence: compute and save the destination, pop into D, then write to the saved address. This extra choreography is why pop typically uses more assembly instructions than push and why translators rely on temporary registers.

keyIdea.title: Pop pattern
keyIdea.text: Compute and save the destination address first (e.g., R13), then pop the top of stack and write it to the saved address.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Pop local/argument/this/that
Canonical pop sequence
Compute destination, save it, pop the stack, then store the popped value.
@index
D=A
@LCL
D=M+D    // D = LCL + index
@R13
M=D      // save target address in R13
@SP
AM=M-1
D=M      // D = popped value
@R13
A=M
M=D      // store value at target
R13 is a temporary register used to preserve the computed address while we pop the value into D.
Explanation bullets
  • Compute the target address and store it in R13 to avoid losing it during the pop.
  • Decrement SP and read the top value into D.
  • Use the saved address to write D into the desired memory location.
  • Pop requires more instructions because you must preserve an address across the pop operation.
Misconception check

Trying to compute the address after popping can overwrite registers and produce incorrect writes. Save the address first.

screens.title: Pointer Segment: Manipulating THIS and THAT
screens.narratorSegment: The pointer segment provides direct access to the base addresses for the this and that segments. It is mapped to R A M addresses three and four: pointer 0 corresponds to R A M[3] (THIS), and pointer 1 corresponds to R A M[4] (THAT). When you push pointer i, you read R A M[3 + i] and push that value; when you pop pointer i, you pop a value and write it to R A M[3 + i], thereby changing the base address used by subsequent this/that accesses. This is useful when working with objects or arrays: setting a pointer updates where object fields resolve. A concrete example: if your translator sees pop pointer 0 and the popped value is 3000, the effect is updating THIS to 3000 so future push this 0 reads from R A M[3000]. A common mistake is confusing pointer with this/that: pointer manipulates the base addresses, not the fields themselves. When implementing, treat pointer as a fixed-address segment similar to temp, but remember its semantic role in controlling base registers. Test pointer operations by pushing known addresses and using them immediately in subsequent this/that accesses to verify correctness.

keyIdea.title: Pointer role
keyIdea.text: Pointer items read or write RAM[3] and RAM[4], changing the base addresses used by the this and that segments.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Pointer Segment
Pointer mapping
Pointer indexes 0 and 1 control the THIS and THAT base addresses respectively.
push pointer 0
Read RAM[3] (THIS) and push to stack.
pop pointer 1
Pop top of stack and write it to RAM[4] (THAT), changing THAT's base address.
Why this matters
Pointer updates are how code adjusts object or array base addresses at runtime. They are essential for field access after a constructor or pointer arithmetic.
Check your understanding
If pop pointer 0 sets THIS to 3000, what will push this 0 return immediately afterwards?

screens.title: Temp Segment: Fixed Temporary Slots
screens.narratorSegment: The temp segment is a block of fixed R A M locations reserved for temporary storage and mapped from R A M[5] upwards. Each temp index i corresponds to R A M[5 + i], so temp 0 maps to R A M[5], temp 7 to R A M[12]. Because these addresses are fixed, translating push temp i and pop temp i is straightforward: read or write the concrete R A M address without computing base plus index. This simplicity is useful for translators because it avoids additional arithmetic when accessing temp. A practical pitfall to avoid is indexing beyond the allowed range — the temp segment covers a fixed set of addresses and is not a general-purpose stack. Use the temp segment for short-lived intermediate values generated by the translator. For testing, push a constant and then pop it into temp 2, then read R A M[7] in the simulator to confirm the correct value. Remember that temp addresses are shared across functions and translations must not assume a per-function frame for temp; they are global fixed slots within this address range.

keyIdea.title: Temp mapping
keyIdea.text: Temp uses fixed RAM slots from addresses 5 through 12, making access a direct address operation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Temp Segment
Fixed addresses for temp
Temp saves translator-temporary values in fixed RAM slots.
temp 0 → RAM[5]
temp 1 → RAM[6]
...
temp 7 → RAM[12]
Access is implemented by using the fixed RAM address; no base register arithmetic is necessary.
Practical note
Because temp addresses are global and fixed, use them only for short-lived intermediate values produced by the translator, not for function-local persistent state.
Check

To verify, pop into temp 2 and inspect RAM[7] in the simulator to see the stored value.

screens.title: Static Segment: Global per-class variables
screens.narratorSegment: The static segment stores class-level variables that persist for the lifetime of the program and are shared across instances. The hardware mapping begins at R A M address sixteen: static variables are assigned addresses starting from R A M[16 + index]. Translators ensure different classes do not collide by using a naming convention that includes the class name and index, for example ClassName. index, and by allocating addresses or offseting by class when appropriate. In practice the VM translator maintains a mapping from each static variable name to a unique R A M slot, starting at 16. A concrete test is to allocate Foo.0 and Bar.0 and observe they map to different addresses so their values do not overwrite each other. Remember that static variables are global, not tied to a call frame; they do not move when you call or return from functions. When implementing, ensure your translator uses consistent naming and allocation across all VM files so static semantics match the language expectations. A common error is treating static like local memory, causing unexpected persistence or collisions between classes.

keyIdea.title: Static allocation
keyIdea.text: Static variables are allocated from RAM[16] upward and are distinguished by class to avoid collisions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Static Segment
Statics start at RAM[16]
Each class's static variables are assigned unique addresses starting from 16 to implement class-level storage.
Naming convention
Use ClassName.index to distinguish static variables in different classes so addresses do not collide.
Persistence
Static variables live for the entire program and are shared across instances of a class.
Implementation note
The translator must coordinate static allocation across VM files to prevent different classes from using the same RAM addresses.
Key Takeaway

Treat static as globally allocated per-class slots beginning at address 16 and maintain a consistent mapping in the translator.

screens.title: Push vs Pop: Instruction cost and asymmetry
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference in complexity between push and pop is central to writing correct and efficient translation code. Push operations are typically shorter: compute the source address (if any), read the value into D, write it at R A M[SP], and increment SP. Pop operations commonly require computing the destination address first and saving it because the stack pop will consume registers needed to hold that address. The translator uses a temporary register like R13 to hold the computed destination while it performs the pop. This adds extra instructions and makes pop more expensive. For example, push local i might need five or six instructions; pop local i usually requires eight or nine. The practical implication is that popping into memory is heavier than pushing from memory, which affects how you design code generation and optimize translator passes. A misconception to avoid is assuming both operations are symmetrical. Instead, remember that the pop's need to preserve the destination address across the stack access is the root cause of the asymmetry. When coding, ensure your translator uses R13 or an equivalent temporary to keep the destination safe until the popped value is retrieved and stored.

keyIdea.title: Asymmetry
keyIdea.text: Pop is more expensive because you must compute and save the destination address before popping the value from the stack.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Push vs Pop
Push (simpler)
Typical steps: compute source, read value, write to stack, increment SP.
Push often needs five to six instructions and does not require saving a destination address before the operation.
Pop (costly)
Typical steps: compute destination, save it (R13), pop stack into D, write D to saved address.
Pop commonly uses extra instructions to preserve the address, making it more complex and slower than push.
Practical consequence
When optimizing or debugging your translator, expect more assembly lines for pop operations and check that the temporary register is not accidentally reused during the sequence.

screens.title: Testing examples: push/pop scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: Testing is crucial. The chapter provides two small VM programs that exercise constants, local variables, and pointer manipulation. The first program pushes constants and pops them into local slots, then reads the locals and adds them. This verifies that push constant and pop local work and that local addressing is correct. The second program manipulates the pointer: it pushes constants and pops them into pointer 0 and pointer 1, then pushes this 0 and that 0 and adds them, confirming that updating pointer changes base addresses for this and that. When you run your translator on these programs, load the generated assembly into the C P U simulator and step through the instructions while watching R A M addresses like SP, LCL, THIS, and THAT. A concrete test step is to confirm that after popping a constant into pointer 0, a subsequent push this 0 returns the value you stored. If a test fails, inspect the sequences for address computation and temporary register usage. These tests are small but exercise the essential mapping and the pop address-saving pattern you implemented.

screens.title: Translator Strategy: Implementing push/pop in your VM translator
screens.narratorSegment: This screen outlines a practical implementation plan you can follow when adding push and pop to your VM translator. Start by implementing push constant because it is the simplest and gives you immediate feedback. Next implement push for base-plus-index segments reusing the same address-computation code for local, argument, this and that by parameterizing the base register. Then implement pop for one base-plus-index segment, following the compute-and-save-address pattern with R13; once pop local works, generalize to argument, this and that. Add pointer and temp as fixed-address handlers — pointer modifies R A M[3 or 4], temp reads or writes R A M[5 + i]. Implement static handling by mapping ClassName. index to R A M[16 + offset] and keep a small table in your translator for assignment. Throughout, write unit tests: push then pop to a fixed R A M address, and run the provided test programs. When debugging, step through assembly in the simulator to inspect SP and the specific R A M addresses you are targeting. Finally, add clear comments in the generated assembly so you can trace which VM command produced which instruction sequence. This incremental plan reduces errors and isolates bugs quickly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Translator Strategy
Step-by-step plan
  1. Implement push constant and verify in simulator.
  2. Add push for base-plus-index segments using a reusable address computation helper.
  3. Implement pop for local using R13 to save the computed destination address.
  4. Generalize pop to argument, this, and that; add pointer and temp handlers.
  5. Implement static allocation mapping starting at RAM[16] with class-scoped names.
  6. Create small VM tests and iterate until the simulator shows correct RAM values.
Debug checklist
  • Does push write to RAM[SP] and increment SP?
  • Does pop compute and save the destination before popping?
  • Are static variables uniquely named per class?
  • Do pointer updates reflect in subsequent this/that accesses?
Key Takeaway

Implement incrementally and test often; address computation and temporary saving are the two places bugs hide.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: To close, carry three concise reminders into your implementation work. First, always map a segment to its correct R A M region — the translator's correctness depends on this mapping. Second, treat constant as virtual: do not attempt memory reads for constant pushes. Third, use a temporary register to save destination addresses when popping: this pattern prevents overwriting values and is the main cause of pop's extra instructions. Keep these rules in mind as quick debugging heuristics: if values go missing, check whether the destination address was saved; if constants behave strangely, ensure they were not treated as R A M reads. These three reminders will speed debugging and keep your translator's semantics faithful to the VM specification. Which one will you check first when a test fails? keyIdea.text: Map segments carefully, treat constant as virtual, and save destination addresses before popping.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What to Remember
Map segments
Ensure each segment uses its intended RAM addresses or base register.
Constant is virtual
Do not issue RAM reads for constant; embed the value in the instruction sequence.
Save pop destination
Compute destination address first and store it (e.g., R13) before popping the value.
Final thought

These three rules are practical checks when implementing and debugging your VM translator's memory access commands.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how VM push and pop commands move data between the stack and named memory segments on the Hack platform. We'll make the mapping from virtual segments — local, argument, this, that, pointer, temp and static — to concrete R A M addresses clear, and you'll see why pushing a value is simpler than popping one. You'll study the assembly patterns used by a VM translator: how to compute base-plus-index addresses, how to write and read the stack, and how the translator uses a temporary register to solve pop's extra step. A practical outcome is that you will be able to implement push and pop for all segments and test them using the provided VM programs. Along the way we'll highlight common misconceptions, such as thinking the constant segment lives in R A M or that pop and push cost the same number of instructions. By the end, you should be confident mapping VM commands to assembly and explaining the asymmetry that makes pop more complex. Consider how a stack-based translator forces explicit address calculation — that idea will keep returning in later chapters.

This first objectives screen prepares you for the practical work ahead. First, you will implement the VM memory access commands push and pop so your translator moves values correctly between the stack and memory. That skill matters because functions, arguments, and object fields all depend on accurate memory access. A concrete example is translating a call to push local 2: it becomes assembly that computes LCL plus two, reads the value, and places it on the stack. Second, you will map every VM memory segment to its hardware location. Knowing that temp begins at R A M address five and that static variables begin at sixteen lets you generate fixed address code without guessing. These two objectives together let you produce correct assembly for a program's variable handling. A common misconception is to treat every segment identically; instead, segments differ in whether they are virtual, base-plus-index, fixed addresses, or per-class allocations. By mastering these two objectives you'll be positioned to implement and test push/pop across all segments.

On this second objectives screen we'll deepen the practical expectations. You will learn to generate the exact assembly patterns for each push and pop variant, including the sequence of instructions to compute base addresses, read or write values, and update SP. For example, pushing from local requires loading LCL, adding the index, reading the value, and then writing it at R A M[SP] before incrementing SP; you'll produce that code reliably. You will also practice the pop sequence: compute and save the destination address in a temporary register, pop the topmost value from the stack into D, then store D at the saved address. This pattern avoids losing either the address or the value. Finally, you will test your translator with small VM programs that exercise constants, pointer adjustments, and local moves. A typical mistake is forgetting to use a temporary register for pop, which leads to wrong destination writes. Mastering these objectives ensures your translator produces correct and debuggable assembly.

Begin by defining the named VM memory segments and their hardware mapping. The VM defines segments like local, argument, this and that as regions addressed by a base register plus an index. For example, local maps to R A M at address LCL plus index — written conceptually as R A M[LCL + index]. Argument similarly maps to R A M[ARG + index]. The pointer and temp segments instead map to fixed R A M addresses: pointer maps to R A M[3] and R A M[4] for index zero and one; temp begins at R A M[5] with offsets for each index. The static segment is special: it is a class-level collection mapped starting at R A M[16]. Static variables are given unique addresses and shared across instances of the same class. Finally, constant is a virtual segment — there is no R A M backing it. Pushing a constant creates the value in the instruction stream, not by reading memory. A useful mental model is labeled drawers: base-plus-offset drawers for local/argument/this/that, fixed-slot drawers for temp and pointer, and a global shelf starting at 16 for static. A common misconception is assuming constant must be read from memory; instead it is supplied directly. Think about why those differences exist: fixed slots are simple for temporary storage, base-plus-index supports variable-length frames, and static persists across calls. How will this mapping affect the translation code you write?

Pushing a constant illustrates how a virtual segment works. There is no memory read because the value is supplied by the VM command itself. The translation pattern loads the constant into the D register, writes D to the address pointed by SP, and then increments SP. Concretely, the translator emits assembly that places the numeric value into A, sets D to A, writes D into R A M[SP], and then increments SP. This is efficient because no base or index computation is needed. A common example is push constant 7: the translator simply creates the value seven and pushes it. A common misconception is trying to treat constant like static or local and reading R A M; that is unnecessary and incorrect. Practically, when you implement this, ensure the code uses A and D registers safely and always increments SP after storing the value. The visual code block shows the canonical assembly sequence so you can copy the pattern into your translator and test it. After testing, ask yourself why this pattern is shorter than most pop sequences and what that implies about runtime cost.

Pushing from base-plus-index segments involves a predictable sequence: compute the address base plus index, read the value from that computed address into D, write D to the stack at SP, and increment SP. The base register might be LCL, ARG, THIS, or THAT depending on the segment. For example, push local 3 becomes code that loads LCL into D, adds the constant three to set A to LCL + 3, then reads M into D and pushes it. The essential steps are address computation, value read, stack store, and SP increment. When you implement this in your translator, avoid overwriting registers you still need; use the D register for intermediate values and use the A register to address memory. A common mistake is performing A=D+A while A is not set correctly — always ensure the base is in D or M as your chosen pattern requires. Another pitfall is forgetting to return A to the stack address before writing D. Test pushes by pushing known locals and then popping them to a fixed R A M slot to observe the values. This pattern is robust and repeated across multiple segments, which means once you implement one, it is straightforward to adapt for others.

Popping a value into a base-plus-index destination is more involved than pushing. The core problem is that computing the destination address and retrieving the popped value both require registers, but you cannot hold both in D simultaneously while addressing memory. The standard solution is to compute base + index, store that computed address in a temporary register such as R13, then pop the stack into D, and finally write D into the saved address. Concretely, you place the index into D, add LCL to get the target address, store that address in R13, decrement SP and move the popped value into D, then set A to R13 and store D there. This sequence guarantees you don't lose either piece of data. A common misconception is thinking you can compute the address after popping; doing so risks overwriting registers used to pop the value. When implementing, ensure you follow the sequence: compute and save the destination, pop into D, then write to the saved address. This extra choreography is why pop typically uses more assembly instructions than push and why translators rely on temporary registers.

The pointer segment provides direct access to the base addresses for the this and that segments. It is mapped to R A M addresses three and four: pointer 0 corresponds to R A M[3] (THIS), and pointer 1 corresponds to R A M[4] (THAT). When you push pointer i, you read R A M[3 + i] and push that value; when you pop pointer i, you pop a value and write it to R A M[3 + i], thereby changing the base address used by subsequent this/that accesses. This is useful when working with objects or arrays: setting a pointer updates where object fields resolve. A concrete example: if your translator sees pop pointer 0 and the popped value is 3000, the effect is updating THIS to 3000 so future push this 0 reads from R A M[3000]. A common mistake is confusing pointer with this/that: pointer manipulates the base addresses, not the fields themselves. When implementing, treat pointer as a fixed-address segment similar to temp, but remember its semantic role in controlling base registers. Test pointer operations by pushing known addresses and using them immediately in subsequent this/that accesses to verify correctness.

The temp segment is a block of fixed R A M locations reserved for temporary storage and mapped from R A M[5] upwards. Each temp index i corresponds to R A M[5 + i], so temp 0 maps to R A M[5], temp 7 to R A M[12]. Because these addresses are fixed, translating push temp i and pop temp i is straightforward: read or write the concrete R A M address without computing base plus index. This simplicity is useful for translators because it avoids additional arithmetic when accessing temp. A practical pitfall to avoid is indexing beyond the allowed range — the temp segment covers a fixed set of addresses and is not a general-purpose stack. Use the temp segment for short-lived intermediate values generated by the translator. For testing, push a constant and then pop it into temp 2, then read R A M[7] in the simulator to confirm the correct value. Remember that temp addresses are shared across functions and translations must not assume a per-function frame for temp; they are global fixed slots within this address range.

The static segment stores class-level variables that persist for the lifetime of the program and are shared across instances. The hardware mapping begins at R A M address sixteen: static variables are assigned addresses starting from R A M[16 + index]. Translators ensure different classes do not collide by using a naming convention that includes the class name and index, for example ClassName. index, and by allocating addresses or offseting by class when appropriate. In practice the VM translator maintains a mapping from each static variable name to a unique R A M slot, starting at 16. A concrete test is to allocate Foo.0 and Bar.0 and observe they map to different addresses so their values do not overwrite each other. Remember that static variables are global, not tied to a call frame; they do not move when you call or return from functions. When implementing, ensure your translator uses consistent naming and allocation across all VM files so static semantics match the language expectations. A common error is treating static like local memory, causing unexpected persistence or collisions between classes.

Understanding the difference in complexity between push and pop is central to writing correct and efficient translation code. Push operations are typically shorter: compute the source address (if any), read the value into D, write it at R A M[SP], and increment SP. Pop operations commonly require computing the destination address first and saving it because the stack pop will consume registers needed to hold that address. The translator uses a temporary register like R13 to hold the computed destination while it performs the pop. This adds extra instructions and makes pop more expensive. A misconception to avoid is assuming both operations are symmetrical. Instead, remember that the pop's need to preserve the destination address across the stack access is the root cause of the asymmetry. When coding, ensure your translator uses R13 or an equivalent temporary to keep the destination safe until the popped value is retrieved and stored.

A concrete test step is to confirm that after popping a constant into pointer 0, a subsequent push this 0 returns the value you stored. If a test fails, inspect the sequences for address computation and temporary register usage. These tests are small but exercise the essential mapping and the pop address-saving pattern you implemented.
